data.name: Pokedex
data.summary: Pokedex for 8 generations of pokemon using PokeAPI.

content:
Pokémon was one of the first cartoons I ever watched, and it stayed with me through collecting cards and playing FireRed and Emerald on my Game Boy. I didn't plan this project with a wireframe or feature list. I just imagined what a Pokedex should feel like and kept coding until it matched.

The app uses live data from PokeAPI inside a pixel-art-inspired interface. You can search for any Pokémon by name, filter the list by type or generation, and view each Pokémon's stats in Chart.js charts. Sprites are lazy-loaded for smoother browsing, and a scroll-to-top button makes long lists easier to navigate.

It also earned my very first GitHub star, so it holds a special place for me.

data.name: Valorant tracker
data.summary: Valorant match history and statistics tracker.

content:
I've played Valorant since Act 1, and the climb from Silver to Ascendant introduced me to some genuinely great people. I built this tracker because tracker.gg didn't show some of the stats I wanted, like kills per weapon and ability usage per agent.

You can search for a player by their name#tag and see their level, current rank, peak rank, and rank progress at the end of each competitive act. Match history shows RR gained or lost, rank at the time, map, and final score.

Each 5v5 match includes per-player stats such as score, kills, deaths, assists, shot placement, AFK rounds, average credits spent, ability usage, and the weapon used for each kill. Round history shows every round's result and bomb plant site.

I also added a "Baiter" stat just for fun. It tracks the most times a player was left as the last one alive while multiple enemies were still up.

data.name: LocalBee
data.summary: World map to track places I have visited and store their photos.

content:
I love traveling and photographing old monuments, quiet nature trails, and anything with character. Over time, the photos piled up with no easy way to remember where I took them or what I thought of each place.

LocalBee is my personal travel map. I can add a place with its coordinates, name, description, rating, image links, and tags, and it appears as a pin on an interactive Leaflet map. Places can be edited, deleted, or filtered by tag.

I found Leaflet while looking through a senior's resume, and it turned out to be exactly the kind of lightweight, flexible library this project needed.

data.name: Cineverse
data.summary: Movie and series collection with rating, plot & cast information using OMDb API.

content:
As a fairly committed binge-watcher, I was always hopping between sites to check a rating or remember the plot of something I'd half-heard about. Cineverse brings that into one place.

You can search for movies and TV series, open a modal with the plot, ratings, and other details, and add or remove titles from a personal watchlist. Toast notifications confirm watchlist changes, and the app supports light and dark mode.

I built the modal and horizontal-scrolling movie list from scratch, without a prebuilt library. That was one of the more demanding frontend challenges I'd taken on at the time, and working with the OMDb API taught me how to fetch and structure data efficiently.

This was my first complete frontend project, and I wanted it to be about something I actually cared about. Since 2022, I've grown over 20 plants from saplings, researching the soil, sunlight, and watering each one needs.

FloraGhar is a responsive plant nursery website with categories for seeds, plants, pots, and accessories. Product pages include prices and care information, such as light requirements, watering frequency, and the kind of space each plant suits.

The search, sorting, and filters are designed with beginners in mind, so someone with no plant knowledge can find what works for their space. It also has a shopping cart and interactive sliders for product images and customer reviews.

data.name: Blogeez
data.summary: Website to read, upload, edit & delete blogs with authentication.

content:
Blogeez was my first full-stack application and my move beyond frontend-only projects. I wanted to understand how authentication and CRUD operations work end to end, rather than just importing a library and trusting it to work.

Users can create accounts, publish, edit, and delete their own posts, and browse posts and profiles from other users. Each profile has a "My Blogs" section showing everything that user has uploaded.

Passwords are hashed with bcrypt. JWTs handle signing and verifying session tokens, cookie-parser handles the cookies, and Axios handles requests between the client and server.

It never reached a deployed final version, but by the time it was done, it felt like I'd built my own miniature version of Reddit from scratch.

data.name: VocalOps
data.summary: An AI-powered voice and CLI interface for local database management.

content:
Why I built it

At my first internship, at Varak Welfare Society, I joined as a React.js intern but soon got pulled into backend work with Django and SQL. Around the same time, I'd installed my first Linux distro, Fedora, so I ended up querying the database from the terminal instead of using a GUI tool.

Over time, that got repetitive. I kept digging through multiple tables just to check whether an integration or workflow had actually succeeded. That gave me the idea for VocalOps, a way to query any local database with my voice, with an LLM routing each request and orchestrating the rest of the workflow. As soon as the internship ended, I started building.

v1 used an older 7B Ollama model and could only query the one database I'd been testing against since day one. Speech-to-text needed API keys, so it was never fully local. It also had a fair number of bugs, and I wouldn't have wanted to use its UI every day. After I joined Mentoria, I put it on hold until I had a clearer idea of what "better" looked like and the skills to build it.

Four months later, I came back for v2. It finally matched what I'd pictured, with a UI for switching between local databases, natural-language queries that work fully offline or with an online Boost mode, and a human-in-the-loop workflow so nothing gets written without my say-so.

{{VOCALOPS_DEMO_VIDEO}}

Architecture

{{VOCALOPS_ARCH_DIAGRAM}}

Connecting a database

Running init validates the file on a read-only connection and scans it into a schema manifest. The manifest stores tables, columns, keys, foreign keys, common column values, redacted sample rows, and a schema hash. It also records whether each table is safe to edit, and why if it isn't.

VocalOps keeps its history, undo log, and LangGraph checkpoints in a separate folder, so it never adds tables to your database.

Reading data

Each request enters a LangGraph state machine with five nodes. A router LLM chooses from eight tools, four for reads and four for proposing writes. Plain Python then sends the request down the correct path.

For a read, VocalOps picks the relevant tables first. Databases with more than 10 tables use Chroma to find the eight closest matches, then add their foreign-key neighbours. The LLM writes one SELECT, and sqlglot parses it into an abstract syntax tree to check the statement type, tables, and columns. Any error goes back to the LLM, with up to three attempts.

The query then runs on a read-only connection with a row limit and a timeout. sqlglot gives the LLM useful feedback, but the read-only connection is what actually prevents writes.

Writing data

{{VOCALOPS_WRITE_DIAGRAM}}

Write tools never write. Updates use a separate, always-local model that returns strict JSON, and the tool validates it before building a preview. The preview shows the affected rows, records their primary keys, and warns about cascading deletes.

LangGraph then saves its state and pauses before commit_mutation. There is no path back to the LLM, so it can't approve its own proposal. Broad or destructive changes also need typed confirmation.

{{VOCALOPS_APPROVAL_IMAGE}}

After approval, the commit step confirms that the matching rows are still the ones I approved. If anything changed, it aborts.

Undo

The undo log and target database are separate files, so each entry starts as pending and becomes committed after the write succeeds. If a crash leaves it pending, undo refuses to run until vocalops undo --repair resolves it. Undoing a change goes through the same preview and approval flow, and supports the last 10 changes of up to 100 rows each.

Voice, UI, and safety

Local speech-to-text runs on faster-whisper, with Deepgram available as an online option. Voice activity detection stops recording after a second of silence, and you can edit the transcript before sending it. The React UI streams answers and includes approval, schema, history, and database-switching views.

The API binds to localhost and uses a CORS allowlist and a per-install bearer token. Boost mode can use Groq for routing, but updates and embeddings stay local.

Testing

Unit tests use a fake LLM to drive the real graph through approvals, rejections, and undo. Three eval suites cover 49 LLM cases, plus one deterministic undo check. They verify routing, approval pauses, row changes, unrelated tables, and undo.

In single-pass runs, local Qwen2.5 7B passed 25 of 30 held-out cases and 11 of 14 hard cases.

data.name: ProductWizz
data.summary: An AI-powered shopping assistant browser extension for amazon.in & flipkart.com.

content:
Why I built it

When I research a product on Amazon or Flipkart, I usually get stuck scrolling through reviews after checking the price. I want to know what buyers think and what problems or benefits they ran into.

So I thought, what if a Chrome extension scraped up to 100 reviews and let an LLM answer my questions from them? That became ProductWizz. Now I can just ask what people think about a specific part of a product instead of scrolling through hundreds of reviews.

{{PRODUCTWIZZ_DEMO_VIDEO}}

What changed in v2

v1 worked, but using it regularly showed its limits. The chat lived in a popup that disappeared too easily, and closing it could interrupt extraction. Answers appeared all at once, and I couldn't see which reviews they came from.

The biggest bug was in storage. Every product went into the same Chroma collection, so a question about one product could retrieve another product's reviews.

I rolled out v2 last week to fix these problems. It adds a Side Panel chat that stays open, a background service worker for extraction, streaming answers over SSE, and citations linked to the exact reviews and specs. Each product session now has its own Chroma collection, and map-reduce handles questions about all the reviews. Scraping and retrieval also got better.

{{PRODUCTWIZZ_V2_DEMO_VIDEO}}

Architecture

{{PRODUCTWIZZ_ARCH_DIAGRAM}}

Extraction

The Side Panel only displays the current state. The service worker tracks each job in chrome.storage.session, so closing the panel doesn't lose progress.

Amazon and Flipkart make server-side scraping difficult, so content scripts run inside the user's own tab. The product script returns the title, price, rating, and highlights immediately. It then scrolls the page, opens collapsed sections, and waits for page changes with a MutationObserver.

The review script reads up to 10 pages, removes duplicates, and stops at 100 reviews. If the review page fails or redirects to sign-in, a watchdog falls back to the reviews already collected. Both sites produce the same data format, so the backend doesn't need separate logic for each one.

Ingestion

The service worker sends the data to a local FastAPI server, which loads the embedding model, reranker, and Zephyr-7B once at startup. It creates documents with metadata such as source type, section, and rating, then splits them into 512-character chunks with a 50-character overlap. bge-large-en-v1.5 embeds the chunks into a Chroma collection for that product session.

Cleanup deletes the collection, and a TTL sweep removes abandoned sessions. If the backend restarts and returns a 404, the extension re-ingests the data from Chrome storage and retries.

Answering a question

{{PRODUCTWIZZ_ANSWER_DIAGRAM}}

The embedding model is fast but can miss details such as negation, because it encodes the question and each chunk separately. bge-reranker-large reads them together, which is slower but more precise. So I retrieve 10 chunks cheaply and keep the best five.

Top-five retrieval can't answer "what share of buyers complain about heating?", so aggregate questions use map-reduce across all the reviews instead.

The prompt tells Zephyr to answer only from the supplied context, show both sides when specs and reviews conflict, and say when it doesn't have enough information. Review text is fenced as untrusted data, which reduces the risk of a review hijacking the prompt. Tokens stream over SSE, followed by the sources, and the panel turns those sources into citation chips.

Running it locally

Endpoints use plain def, so FastAPI runs them in a threadpool and health checks stay responsive. A lock allows one generation at a time because the app shares one llama.cpp model. The server binds to localhost, CORS allows only the extension, and inference stays on the machine at temperature 0.2.

data.name: LLM from scratch
data.summary: A complete implementation of GPT model like LLM from scratch with attention, training, fine-tuning and text classification capabilities.

content:
Why I built it

I'd been using LLMs almost daily for studying and planning, but I had no real understanding of what was happening beneath the chat interface. During a break from coursework, that curiosity turned into a project. Instead of just reading about transformers, I wanted to build one myself, line by line.

After researching options across forums and reviews, I landed on Sebastian Raschka's Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch). It came highly recommended, and using PyTorch was an added bonus since I'd been wanting to get comfortable with it anyway.

The repository follows chapters 2 to 7 of the book, so it can also work as a reference for anyone going through the same material. It's currently my highest-starred repository.

Architecture

{{LLM_ARCH_DIAGRAM}}

Preparing the data

I started with simple regex-based tokenizers to see how text becomes token IDs and why unknown words become a problem. I then moved to GPT-2's byte-pair encoding through tiktoken, which can break any string into known pieces.

GPTDatasetV1 creates training examples with a sliding window. The target is the same sequence shifted by one token, so every position in a chunk becomes a next-token prediction.

Building attention

src/attention.py builds attention up in stages, starting with a simple weighted average and ending with an efficient MultiHeadAttention class.

Each token gets learned query, key, and value projections. The scores are scaled, then a causal mask hides future positions so a token can only attend to itself and earlier tokens. GPT-2 small splits its 768 dimensions across 12 heads, which lets each head learn from a different subspace.

The GPT model

Each TransformerBlock combines causal attention and a feed-forward network, with LayerNorm applied before each one and residual connections around both. The residual paths help gradients flow through the 12 layers.

I worked out the parameter count by hand to check my understanding. The model has about 163M parameters with a separate output head, and about 124M when that head shares weights with the token embeddings. To verify the architecture, I loaded OpenAI's GPT-2 weights and confirmed that greedy generation matched the book's reference output.

Training and generation

src/train.py contains the training loop, cross-entropy loss utilities, loss plotting, and text generation. Generation supports greedy decoding, temperature, and top-k sampling. I trained and fine-tuned the model on Google Colab and tracked loss curves for both fine-tuning stages.

Fine-tuning

{{LLM_FINETUNE_DIAGRAM}}

For SMS spam detection, I balanced the dataset and replaced the output head with a two-class layer. Only the last transformer block, final LayerNorm, and new head were trained, which is about 5.7% of the model's parameters. The prediction comes from the last token because, with causal attention, it's the only position that can see the entire message.

My first result was 81.33% test accuracy, well below the book's reference. The run reproduced exactly, so I compared the recipes and found one difference. I'd left dropout at 0.1, which kept adding noise to features from frozen layers that couldn't adapt to it. With dropout at 0.0, test accuracy reached 95.67%.

{{CLASSIFICATION_LOSS_IMAGE}}

For instruction following, I formatted 1,100 examples using Alpaca-style prompts and split them into 935 training, 110 test, and 55 validation examples. A custom collate function pads each batch to its own longest sequence. The first end-of-text token stays as a target so the model learns when to stop, while the remaining padding uses -100 and doesn't count toward the loss.

{{INSTRUCTION_FINETUNING_LOSS_IMAGE}}

Project structure

Each file maps directly to a chapter, from tokenization and attention through to both fine-tuning stages. That makes it easy to read the code alongside the book.
